{{For|the dog|Chow Chow}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly in the field of [[algebraic geometry]], a '''Chow variety''' is an [[algebraic variety]] whose points correspond to effective [[algebraic cycles]] of fixed dimension and degree on a given [[projective space]]. More precisely, the Chow variety<ref>The notation for Chow varieties is not standard between references.</ref> <math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n)</math> is the [[moduli space|fine moduli variety]] parametrizing all effective algebraic cycles of dimension <math>k-1</math> and degree <math>d</math> in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>.

The Chow variety <math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n)</math> may be constructed via a '''Chow embedding''' into a sufficiently large projective space. This is a direct generalization of the construction of a [[Grassmannian]] variety via the [[Plücker embedding]], as Grassmannians are the <math>d=1</math> case of Chow varieties.

Chow varieties are distinct from [[Chow groups]], which are the [[abelian group]] of all [[algebraic cycles]] on a variety (not necessarily projective space) up to rational equivalence. Both are named for [[Wei-Liang Chow]] (周煒良), a pioneer in the study of algebraic cycles.

==Background on algebraic cycles==

If X is a closed [[subvariety (algebraic geometry)|subvariety]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> of dimension <math>k-1</math>, the '''degree''' of X is the number of intersection points between X and a generic<ref>Here and throughout, we assume that the base field is algebraically closed and characteristic 0, so we may define 'generic' as any phenomenon characterized by a Zariski open condition. Degree may be defined in larger generality, but counting generic intersections is arguably the most intuitive.</ref> <math>(n-k)</math>-dimensional [[projective subspace]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>.<ref>Note that degree is not intrinsic to X as a variety, but rather to its embedding in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>.</ref>

Degree is constant in families<ref>All families are assumed to be [[flat morphism|flat]].</ref> of subvarieties, except in certain degenerate limits. To see this, consider the following family parametrized by t.
:<math>X_t := V(x^2-tyz) \subset \mathbb{P}^{2}</math>.
Whenever <math>t\neq0</math>, <math>X_t</math> is a conic (an irreducible subvariety of degree 2), but <math>X_0</math> degenerates to the line <math>x=0</math> (which has degree 1). There are several approaches to reconciling this issue, but the simplest is to declare <math>X_0</math> to be a ''line of multiplicity 2'' (and more generally to attach multiplicities to subvarieties) using the language of ''algebraic cycles''.

A <math>(k-1)</math>-dimensional '''[[algebraic cycle]]''' is a finite formal linear combination
:<math>X=\sum_{i} m_{i}X_{i}</math>.
in which <math>X_{i}</math>s are <math>(k-1)</math>-dimensional irreducible closed subvarieties in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>, and <math>m_{i}</math>s are integers. An algebraic cycle is '''effective''' if each <math>m_i\geq0</math>. The '''degree''' of an algebraic cycle is defined to be 
:<math>\deg(X):=\sum_{i} m_{i}\deg(X_{i})</math>. 

A [[homogeneous polynomial]] or [[homogeneous ideal]] in n-many variables defines an effective algebraic cycle in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>, in which the multiplicity of each irreducible component is the order of vanishing at that component. In the family of algebraic cycles defined by <math>x^2-tyz</math>, the <math>t=0</math> cycle is 2 times the line  <math>x=0</math>, which has degree 2. More generally, the degree of an algebraic cycle is constant in families, and so it makes sense to consider the [[moduli problem]] of effective algebraic cycles of fixed dimension and degree.

==Examples of Chow varieties==

There are three special classes of Chow varieties with particularly simple constructions.

===Degree 1: Subspaces===

An effective algebraic cycle in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> of dimension k-1 and degree 1 is the projectivization of a k-dimensional subspace of n-dimensional affine space. This gives an isomorphism to a [[Grassmannian]] variety:
:<math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,1,n) \simeq \operatorname{Gr}(k,n)</math>
The latter space has a distinguished system of [[homogeneous coordinates]], given by the [[Plücker coordinates]].

===Dimension 0: Points===

An effective algebraic cycle in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> of dimension 0 and degree d is an (unordered) d-tuple of points in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>, possibly with repetition. This gives an isomorphism to a [[symmetric power]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>:
:<math>\operatorname{Gr}(1,d,n) \simeq \operatorname{Sym}_d\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>.

===Codimension 1: Divisors===

An effective algebraic cycle in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> of codimension 1<ref>An algebraic cycle of codimension 1 is also called a [[Weil divisor]].</ref> and degree d can be defined by the vanishing of a single degree d polynomial in n-many variables, and this polynomial is unique up to rescaling. Letting <math>V_{d,n}</math> denote the vector space of degree d polynomials in n-many variables, this gives an isomorphism to a [[projective space]]:
:<math>\operatorname{Gr}(n-1,d,n) \simeq \mathbb{P}V_{d,n}</math>.
Note that the latter space has a distinguished system of [[homogeneous coordinates]], which send a polynomial to the coefficient of a fixed monomial.

===A non-trivial example===

The Chow variety <math>\operatorname{Gr}(2,2,4)</math> parametrizes dimension 1, degree 2 cycles in <math>\mathbb{P}^{3}</math>. This Chow variety has two irreducible components.
{{bulleted list 
|The moduli of conics contained in a projective plane (and their degenerations).
|The moduli of pairs of lines.
}}
These two 8-dimensional components intersect in the moduli of coplanar pairs of lines, which is the singular locus in <math>\operatorname{Gr}(2,2,4)</math>. This shows that, in contrast with the special cases above, Chow varieties need not be smooth or irreducible. 

==The Chow embedding==

Let X be an irreducible subvariety in <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> of dimension k-1 and degree d. By the definition of the degree, most <math>(n-k)</math>-dimensional [[projective subspace|projective subspaces]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> intersect X in d-many points. By contrast, most <math>(n-k-1)</math>-dimensional [[projective subspace|projective subspaces]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> do not intersect at X at all. This can be sharpened as follows.

'''Lemma.'''<ref>[GKZ94, Chapter 3, Proposition 2.2]</ref> The set <math>Z(X) \subset \operatorname{Gr}(n-k,n)</math> parametrizing the subspaces of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> which intersect X non-trivially is an irreducible hypersurface of degree<ref>'Degree' has only been defined in this article for subvarieties of projective space. However, the [[Plucker coordinates]] allow an analogous definition of degree for subvarieties of Grassmannians.</ref> d.

As a consequence, there exists a degree d form<ref>A ''degree d form'' in this context means a [[homogeneous coordinate]] of degree d. For a Grassmannian, this can be given by a degree d polynomial in the Plücker coordinates, and is well-defined up to the Plücker relations.</ref> <math>R_X</math> on <math>\operatorname{Gr}(n-k,n)</math> which vanishes precisely on <math>Z(X)</math>, and this form is unique up to scaling. This construction can be extended to an algebraic cycle <math>X=\sum_{i} m_{i}X_{i}</math> by declaring that <math>R_X:= \prod_{i} R_{X_i}^{m_i}</math>. To each degree d algebraic cycle, this associates a degree d form <math>R_X</math> on <math>\operatorname{Gr}(n-k,n)</math>, called the '''Chow form''' of X, which is well-defined up to scaling.

Let <math>V_{k,d,n}</math> denote the vector space of degree d forms on <math>\operatorname{Gr}(n-k,n)</math>.

'''The Chow-van-der-Waerden Theorem.'''<ref>cf. [GKZ94, Chapter 4, Theorem 1.1]</ref> The map <math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}V_{k,d,n}</math> which sends <math>X\mapsto R_X</math> is a closed embedding of varieties.

In particular, an effective algebraic cycle X is determined by its Chow form <math>R_X</math>. 

If a basis for <math>V_{k,d,n}</math> has been chosen, sending <math>X</math> to the coefficients of <math>R_X</math> in this basis gives a system of homogeneous coordinates on the Chow variety <math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n)</math>, called the '''Chow coordinates''' of <math>X</math>. However, as there is no consensus as to the ‘best’ basis for <math>V_{k,d,n}</math>, this term can be ambiguous.

From a foundational perspective, the above theorem is usually used as the definition of <math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n)</math>. That is, the Chow variety is usually defined as a subvariety of <math>\mathbb{P}V_{k,d,n}</math>, and only then shown to be a fine moduli space for the moduli problem in question.

==Relation to the Hilbert scheme==

A more sophisticated solution to the problem of 'correctly' counting the degree of a degenerate subvariety is to work with [[scheme (mathematics)|subschemes]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> rather than subvarieties. Schemes can keep track of [[infinitesimal]] information that varieties and algebraic cycles cannot.

For example, if two points in a variety approach each other in an algebraic family, the limiting subvariety is a single point, the limiting algebraic cycle is a point with multiplicity 2, and the limiting subscheme is a 'fat point' which contains the tangent direction along which the two points collided.

The '''[[Hilbert scheme]]''' <math>\operatorname{Hilb}(k,d,n)</math> is the [[fine moduli scheme]] of closed subschemes of dimension k-1 and degree d inside <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>.<ref>There is considerable variance in how the term 'Hilbert scheme' is used. Some authors don't subdivide by dimension or degree, others assume the dimension is 0 (i.e. a Hilbert scheme of points), and still others consider more general schemes than <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>.</ref> Each closed subscheme determines an effective algebraic cycle, and the induced map
:<math>\operatorname{Hilb}(k,d,n) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n)</math>.
is called the '''cycle map''' or the '''Hilbert-Chow morphism'''. This map is generically an isomorphism over the points in <math>\operatorname{Gr}(k,d,n)</math> corresponding to irreducible subvarieties of degree d, but the fibers over non-simple algebraic cycles can be more interesting.

==Chow quotient ==
A '''Chow quotient''' parametrizes closures of [[generic orbit]]s. It is constructed as a closed subvariety of a Chow variety.

Kapranov's theorem says that the [[moduli space of curves|moduli space]] <math>\overline{M}_{0, n}</math> of [[stable curve|stable]] genus-zero curves with ''n'' marked points is the Chow quotient of Grassmannian <math>\operatorname{Gr}(2, \C^n)</math> by the standard maximal torus.
